scope: Operational census of the Nepal/Darjeeling paper experiments reconstructed from the 1842 Journal of the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India correspondence dossier and sequel.

source_control.primary_source: Correspondence relative to the Manufacture of Nipal Paper at Darjeeling, with details as to its cost, relative value, mode of bleaching, and rendering water proof, Journal of the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India 1 (1842), 210-221; sequel, 273-274.
source_control.warning: OCR-derived extraction. Verify exact wording and numerical typography against page images before publication quotation.

records.label: Skilled-maker transfer from Nepal to Darjeeling
observations: Campbell states that Lord Auckland asked Hodgson to send people skilled in Nepali paper manufacture.
Five makers were sent by the Nepal Durbar at Hodgson's request.
Monthly wage hierarchy: head maker Rs 10; mate Rs 8; three ordinary workers Rs 8 each; total Rs 42.
records.analytical_value: Technology moves through differentiated labour, pay, authority and travel rather than as recipe alone.

records.label: Manufactory siting: carriage economy versus experimental observation
observations: Makers preferred Pucheem/Pacheem to economise carriage and remain close to paper-tree supply.
Campbell overrode their preference because he wanted manufacture nearer his own observation.
A small house and tank were built near a stream crossing Auckland Road; water was carried by bamboo conduits.
records.analytical_value: Observability is itself an infrastructural requirement with transport costs.

records.label: Wet-bark transport failure
records.operation: transport dried bark from Pacheem to Darjeeling
observations: Makers insisted bark should be thoroughly dried and not rewetted before use.
Some dried bark became wet during carriage from Pacheem to Darjeeling, mildewed, and was reported altogether useless for paper-making.
records.analytical_value: Raw-material custody and transport conditions are part of paper manufacture.

records.label: Workshop material substitutions and process calibration
records.operation: reconstruct Nepali manufacturing process at Darjeeling
observations: Campbell uses Hodgson's 1832 implement list as baseline.
Makers use a flat stone and double-headed mallets rather than Hodgson's stone mortar and pestle.
Iron boiler is rejected because it darkens paper; tinned copper is preferred, brass considered acceptable.
Continuous water flow through the tank is required to carry alkali away from pulp.
records.interface: portable written specification / tacit workshop practice
records.analytical_value: Recipe transmission reveals local substitutions and tacit knowledge rather than exact replication.

records.label: Campbell bleaching trade-off trials
observations: Immersion plus exposure whitened the pulp considerably but destroyed the toughness characteristic of the untreated paper.
Board exposure preserved toughness but produced little whitening.
Campbell abandoned the immersion plan and proposed further dry-season exposure trials.
records.failure_mode: property trade-off: whitening by immersion -> toughness loss; non-immersion exposure -> insufficient whitening
records.analytical_value: Improvement is multi-dimensional; optimizing colour can destroy strength.

records.label: Distributed bleaching handoff to O'Shaughnessy
observations: Government requested 20-30 sheets in several dak despatches for O'Shaughnessy's experiments.
O'Shaughnessy reported success using chlorine in water instead of chloride of lime.
The process was passed to Marshman at Serampore Paper Mills for practical larger-scale testing.
records.failure_mode: chloride-of-lime interaction with colouring matter -> difficult bleaching
records.interface: Darjeeling workshop / government office / chemical laboratory / industrial mill
records.analytical_value: Failure creates a distributed troubleshooting network rather than ending the experiment.

records.label: Filtering-paper substitution test
observations: Government noted English filtering paper at Rs 9 per ream versus an understood Darjeeling cost of about Rs 3 per ream for that purpose.
Editors later reported that Nepal paper's strength allowed pressure/twisting without tearing.
Actual filtering was slower and produced less clear liquor than good European filtering paper.
records.failure_mode: strength advantage accompanied by slow filtration and poorer clarification
records.analytical_value: A material can rank highly on mechanical strength yet poorly on the full operational requirements of filtration.

records.label: India-rubber waterproof postal-wrap substitution
observations: India-rubber-treated Darjeeling paper was reported perfectly waterproof.
Prepared paper was reported to weigh one-third as much as the same area of Post Office wax cloth.
Post Office authorities proposed substitution to reduce expense and improve packet protection.
records.interface: paper treatment / postal packet / monsoon transport
records.analytical_value: Colour becomes irrelevant while strength, mass and waterproofing become decisive: affordance ranking changes with operation.

records.label: Serampore machine-web affordance reversal
records.operation: adapt bark fibre to machine paper production
observations: Marshman reported little hope of economic success versus alternative materials.
Even after treatments analogous to English paper practice, general paper quality remained inferior.
Mucilaginous material prevented pulp from running freely on the web when greater thickness was attempted.
Marshman doubted general use with machinery then in vogue.
He nevertheless identified strength-dominant applications such as bank-note paper as more plausible.
records.failure_mode: mucilaginous fibre/pulp behaviour -> poor machine-web flow and thickness control; high bleaching/process cost
records.interface: Nepal/Darjeeling bark fibre / Serampore machine web
records.analytical_value: The same fibre behaviour that supports tough hand-made paper becomes a production defect at a machine interface: a direct affordance reversal.

cross_cutting_claims: Affordance is operation- and interface-specific rather than an intrinsic ranking of paper types.
Failed experiments reveal the property bundles and infrastructural interfaces that successful use can hide.
Technology transfer involved skilled bodies, pay, authority, tools, raw materials, specimens, formulas and repeated testing.
Paper manufacture extended into drying, raw-material transport, water supply, fuel/ash ecology and workshop siting.
Finished sheets became distributed experimental objects circulating among Darjeeling, Calcutta and Serampore.
The 1842 editors themselves omitted some document-transmission notes as unimportant, creating a historically revealing contrast with this project's focus on circulation metadata.
